incidents.title: United States federal court bars CNN from broadcasting recordings of Manuel Noriega's calls with his lawyers
incidents.summary: In November 1990, the United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida ordered Cable News Network to stop broadcasting tape recordings of jailed former Panamanian leader Manuel Noriega's telephone conversations with his defense lawyers. The Supreme Court of the United States declined to lift the order on November 18, 1990, over a dissent from Justices Thurgood Marshall and Sandra Day O'Connor.
incidents.what_happened: General Manuel Noriega, a defendant in a pending federal criminal proceeding in Florida, asked the United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida to stop Cable News Network from broadcasting recorded conversations between him and his attorneys. On November 8, 1990, the District Court continued a temporary restraint on the broadcast, and a second written order dated November 9, 1990, kept the restraint in place for up to ten days while the court reviewed the recordings. CNN asked the United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit to lift the order, but the panel denied relief, saying the First Amendment interests of the press and the public would be served by CNN immediately producing the tapes to the District Court rather than broadcasting them. CNN then asked the Supreme Court of the United States to stay the restraining orders and to review the case. On November 18, 1990, the Supreme Court denied both requests. Justice Thurgood Marshall, joined by Justice Sandra Day O'Connor, dissented.
incidents.stated_justification: Manuel Noriega's motion asked the court to prevent Cable News Network from broadcasting the recorded conversations between him and his attorneys.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Rather than clearing Cable News Network to broadcast the recordings, the Eleventh Circuit panel said the First Amendment interests of the press and the public would be served by CNN immediately producing the tapes to the District Court for review.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Manuel Noriega was a defendant in a pending federal criminal proceeding in Florida when Cable News Network obtained recordings of his prison telephone calls with his attorneys.
incidents.outcome_note: The Supreme Court of the United States denied Cable News Network's request to stay the restraining orders and denied its petition for certiorari on November 18, 1990, over a dissent from Justices Thurgood Marshall and Sandra Day O'Connor.

incidents.title: United States Supreme Court strikes down Florida law barring a reporter from discussing his own grand jury testimony
incidents.summary: In 1990, the Supreme Court of the United States struck down a Florida law that threatened newspaper reporter Michael Smith with criminal prosecution for discussing his own testimony before a state grand jury investigating local officials. The Court ruled unanimously that a state may not ban a grand jury witness from disclosing his own testimony once the grand jury's term has ended.
incidents.what_happened: Michael Smith was a reporter for the Charlotte Herald-News in Charlotte County, Florida. While writing a series of newspaper articles, he obtained information about alleged wrongdoing in the Charlotte County State Attorney's Office and Sheriff's Department. A special prosecutor called Smith to testify before a Florida grand jury investigating those allegations. At the time he testified, Smith was warned by the special prosecutor's staff not to reveal his testimony in any manner, and that doing so could result in criminal prosecution under Florida Statute 905.27. After the grand jury ended its investigation, Smith wanted to write about what he had learned, including his own testimony, but the statute still barred him from disclosing it. He sued in federal court, and his case reached the Supreme Court of the United States. On March 21, 1990, the Court held unanimously that Florida's law violated the First Amendment insofar as it barred a grand jury witness from disclosing his own testimony after the grand jury's term had ended.
incidents.stated_justification: The Supreme Court noted that Florida's asserted interests in grand jury secrecy included that if preindictment proceedings were made public, prospective witnesses would be hesitant to come forward voluntarily, knowing that those against whom they testified would be aware of that testimony.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: The Court said the ban's impact on Smith's ability to make a truthful public statement was dramatic, since before testifying he had been free to speak about matters of public concern but believed he could no longer communicate that information.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Smith's reporting concerned alleged wrongdoing inside the Charlotte County State Attorney's Office and Sheriff's Department, which a special prosecutor and a state grand jury were investigating.
incidents.outcome_note: The Supreme Court held unanimously that Florida's ban violated the First Amendment as applied to a witness who wanted to discuss his own testimony after the grand jury's term had ended.

incidents.title: Peru strips television station owner Baruch Ivcher of his citizenship after critical reporting
incidents.summary: In July 1997, the government of President Alberto Fujimori stripped Baruch Ivcher, the Israeli-born owner of Peru's Frecuencia Latina-Canal 2 television station, of his Peruvian citizenship, making him ineligible under Peruvian law to own the station. The Committee to Protect Journalists said it believed the action came "in direct reprisal for investigative reports of Frecuencia Latina-Canal 2."
incidents.what_happened: Baruch Ivcher, who was born in Israel, was a naturalized Peruvian citizen and the majority shareholder of Frecuencia Latina-Canal 2, a television station in Lima, Peru. In 1997, Frecuencia Latina-Canal 2 aired a series of investigative reports about the government of President Alberto Fujimori. In July of that year, the government stripped Ivcher of his Peruvian citizenship, which made him ineligible under Peruvian law to own a television station. The Committee to Protect Journalists, a press freedom organization, said it believed the action was taken "in direct reprisal for investigative reports of Frecuencia Latina-Canal 2, including stories that implicated Peru's intelligence services in the wiretapping of journalists and members of the opposition." Ivcher went into exile in the United States and Israel. Control of the station passed to its minority owners, brothers Mendel and Samuel Winter, after a Peruvian court later convicted an associate of Ivcher's of fraudulently transferring shares of the company.
incidents.stated_justification: The Committee to Protect Journalists said it believed the action was taken "in direct reprisal for investigative reports of Frecuencia Latina-Canal 2, including stories that implicated Peru's intelligence services in the wiretapping of journalists and members of the opposition."
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Ivcher went into exile in the United States and Israel, and majority control of Frecuencia Latina-Canal 2 passed to the station's minority owners, brothers Mendel and Samuel Winter.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Frecuencia Latina-Canal 2's investigative reporting, including stories on alleged government wiretapping of journalists and opposition figures, had drawn friction with the Fujimori government in 1997.
incidents.outcome_note: As of the Committee to Protect Journalists' report on 1999, Ivcher remained in exile and the Winter brothers retained majority control of Frecuencia Latina-Canal 2.

incidents.title: Belarus jails journalist Pavel Sheremet over his reporting for Russian television station ORT
incidents.summary: In 1997, Belarusian authorities under President Alexander Lukashenko jailed journalist Pavel Sheremet for three months in connection with his reporting for the Russian television station ORT. The Committee to Protect Journalists said the same authorities also banned Sheremet from reporting at one point and forbade him from traveling to the West for a year.
incidents.what_happened: Pavel Sheremet worked as a bureau chief for the Russian television station ORT, whose coverage was often critical of authorities, according to the Committee to Protect Journalists. He had earlier edited the independent newspaper Belarusskaya Delovaya Gazeta in his native Belarus. In 1997, Belarusian authorities jailed Sheremet for three months in connection with his reporting for ORT. The Committee to Protect Journalists, a press freedom organization, said the same authorities also banned Sheremet from reporting at one point and forbade him from traveling to the West for a year. In 1998, the organization named Sheremet a CPJ International Press Freedom awardee; for weeks, he and CPJ pressed authorities in Belarus for an exit visa, without which he could not leave Minsk to travel to the award ceremony in the United States. Belarusian authorities later stripped Sheremet of his citizenship in 2010.
incidents.stated_justification: The Committee to Protect Journalists said Sheremet's imprisonment came over investigative journalism he had done for the Russian television channel ORT.
incidents.effect_on_reporting: Belarusian authorities banned Sheremet from reporting at one point and forbade him from traveling to the West for a year, according to the Committee to Protect Journalists.
incidents.issue_of_the_day: Sheremet's reporting on Belarus for ORT was often critical of authorities under President Alexander Lukashenko.
incidents.outcome_note: Belarusian authorities later stripped Sheremet of his Belarusian citizenship in 2010, according to the Committee to Protect Journalists.
